components.note: Originally depicted a burning candle or the sun's rays radiating outward — the source of 白's meaning 'white, bright, clear.'
疒 (sickness) — 痴 was historically viewed as an illness of the mind.
知 (zhī) gives a sound close to chī, sharing the same rhyme and a related initial.

example.hanzi: 别再犯这种白痴的错误了。
example.pinyin: Bié zài fàn zhè zhǒng báichī de cuòwù le.
example.english: Don't make such idiotic mistakes again.
example.fact: 白 here likely contributes the sense of "blank" (an empty mind), while 痴 alone recurs across a family of words for foolish infatuation — 痴迷 ("besotted"), 情痴 ("lovesick fool") — all sharing the illness radical 疒 that frames obsession as a kind of sickness of the mind.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 任 relates to a person taking on a responsibility or role.
壬 (rén) gives a hint of the sound — 任 is pronounced rèn, a connection that has shifted somewhat.

example.hanzi: 我们之间需要更多的信任。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zhījiān xūyào gèng duō de xìnrèn.
example.english: We need more trust between us.
example.fact: 信任 describes trusting a person or institution as reliable over time (信任朋友, "trust a friend"), while 相信 is used for believing a specific statement or fact (相信他的话, "believe what he says") — two different English senses of "trust/believe" that Chinese keeps grammatically distinct.

components.note: 亲 (here representing a tree, related to 榛/hazel) — 新 pictures a tree being cut.
斤 (an axe) — freshly chopping wood gave 新 its meaning of something 'new' or 'fresh.'
耳 (ear) — 闻 originally meant 'to hear,' later extending to 'smell' and 'news.'
门 (mén) contributes the rhyme -en, close to wén's sound, though the initial has since shifted.

example.hanzi: 我每天早上看新闻。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang kàn xīnwén.
example.english: I watch the news every morning.
example.fact: 闻 originally meant simply "to hear" (its ear radical 耳 still shows this) before narrowing to "smell" in isolation and broadening to "news" in compounds — so 新闻, literally "newly heard [things]", preserves the character's oldest sense better than most modern uses of 闻 alone.

components.note: Depicts a young wheat or tree branch that has not yet borne fruit — the image of something still incomplete, the source of 未's meaning 'not yet.'
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.hanzi: 谁也不知道未来会怎样。
example.pinyin: Shéi yě bù zhīdào wèilái huì zěnyàng.
example.english: No one knows what the future will be like.
example.fact: 未来 is built from two transparent time-logic characters: 未 ("not yet") plus 来 ("to come") literally spells out "not-yet-arrived" — the same 未 shows up in 未婚 ("not yet married") and 未成年 ("not yet an adult, i.e. a minor").

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 道 relates to a path or road one walks along.
首 (shǒu) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer resembles dào, a reminder that sound components can drift after thousands of years of pronunciation change.
欠 (lack) — 歉 describes a lack or shortfall, and later, the feeling of owing an apology.
兼 (jiān) gives a sound distantly related to 歉's reading qiàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 他向我道歉了。
example.pinyin: Tā xiàng wǒ dàoqiàn le.
example.english: He apologized to me.
example.fact: 道 carries several unrelated-seeming senses across common words — "road/way" in 道路, "to say" in 道歉 (literally "to speak an apology") and 知道 ("to know"), and "principle" in 道理 — a single character doing a lot of semantic work worth tracking across vocabulary rather than assuming one fixed meaning.

components.note: 丁 (a stylized handle/hook shape in the ancient form) — part of the character's original picture, now mostly opaque in the modern form
口 (kǒu, mouth) gives a sound related to 可's pronunciation kě, and may connect to 可's sense of approval spoken aloud
忄 (heart) shows 怜 relates to an emotion.
令 (lìng) gives a sound close to lián, differing mainly in the vowel and tone.

example.hanzi: 这只小狗看起来很可怜。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhī xiǎo gǒu kànqǐlai hěn kělián.
example.english: This little dog looks so pitiful.
example.fact: 可怜 can switch part of speech without changing form: as an adjective it means "pitiful" (他很可怜, "he's pitiful"), but placed before a person it becomes a verb meaning "to pity" (可怜可怜他, "have some pity on him") — the same two characters doing double grammatical duty.

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 在 originally related to standing on the ground
才 (cái) gives the sound — 在 is pronounced zài, a close match

example.hanzi: 这道题实在太难了。
example.pinyin: Zhè dào tí shízài tài nán le.
example.english: This problem is really too hard.
example.fact: 实在 most often shows up as an intensifying adverb before an adjective ("really, truly" — 实在很难), a usage that has drifted quite far from its literal building blocks 实 ("real, solid") and 在 ("to exist, to be present") — "real and present" becoming, in effect, just "truly".

components.note: 力 (strength) — 加 pictures adding one's effort to a cause.
口 (mouth, words) — combining strength with words of support gave 加 its meaning 'to add' or 'to increase.'
入 depicts a simple wedge or arrow shape pointing inward, showing the direction of entering.

example.hanzi: 他刚加入我们公司。
example.pinyin: Tā gāng jiārù wǒmen gōngsī.
example.english: He just joined our company.
example.fact: 加入 typically takes an organization, group, or activity as its object (加入球队, "join the team") — for joining a single ongoing event already in progress, Chinese usually reaches for 参加 instead, a near-synonym with a narrower, event-focused range.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) — relates directly to 病's meaning 'illness, disease, to be sick.'
丙 (bǐng) gives a sound hint — 病 is pronounced bìng, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 医生正在检查病人。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng zhèngzài jiǎnchá bìngrén.
example.english: The doctor is examining the patient.
example.fact: 病人 is the everyday, spoken word for "patient"; hospitals and medical writing more often use the more formal, clinical-sounding 患者 for the same role — a register split similar to English "patient" versus a chart's "the individual".

components.note: 氵 (water) — 治 relates to managing or controlling the flow of water, such as flood control.
台 (a platform, structure) — a structure used to direct and control water gave 治 its meaning 'to govern' or 'to manage.'
疒 depicts a person lying sick in bed, the 'illness' radical.
了 here depicts a resolving action — clearing away an illness gave 疗 its meaning 'to treat, to cure.'

example.hanzi: 这种病可以治疗。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhǒng bìng kěyǐ zhìliáo.
example.english: This illness can be treated.
example.fact: 治 originally meant "to manage, to govern" (its water radical 氵 points to controlling floods) before extending to the medical sense "to treat" — the same semantic leap from "governing a state" to "governing a body" that English makes when it talks about "managing" a disease.

components.note: 厂 (a cliff or overhang) — 原 relates to a source high up, such as a spring emerging from rock.
泉 (quán) gives a hint of the sound — 原 is pronounced yuán, a connection that has shifted somewhat.
讠 (speech) — 谅 describes speaking with understanding, forgiving in words.
京 (jīng) gives a sound distantly related to 谅's reading liàng, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 请原谅我的错误。
example.pinyin: Qǐng yuánliàng wǒ de cuòwù.
example.english: Please forgive my mistake.
example.fact: 原谅 sits at the personal, everyday end of Chinese's forgiveness vocabulary; its near-synonym 谅解 leans more formal and mutual, closer to "to reach an understanding" than a simple "I forgive you" between friends.

components.note: 彳 depicts a step with the left foot; together with 亍 (a step with the right foot), 行 shows a person walking or moving.
亍 depicts a step with the right foot, complementing 彳 to form the idea of walking or travel.

example.hanzi: 他的行为让大家很惊讶。
example.pinyin: Tā de xíngwéi ràng dàjiā hěn jīngyà.
example.english: His behavior surprised everyone.
example.fact: 为 is a genuine tone-trap: read wéi it means "to act, to do" (as in 行为, "conduct"), but read wèi it means "for, for the sake of" (as in 因为 and 为什么, both in the pilot batch) — same character, same simplified form, two grammatically unrelated jobs depending purely on tone.

components.note: 比 is made of two identical 匕 (spoon) shapes placed side by side — comparing two similar things led to its meaning 'to compare.'
车 (cart/vehicle) — 较 originally related to comparing the crossbars of chariots
交 (jiāo) gives a sound close to 较's reading jiào

example.hanzi: 这个牌子比较贵。
example.pinyin: Zhège páizi bǐjiào guì.
example.english: This brand is relatively expensive.
example.fact: 比较 does double duty just like 可能 elsewhere in this deck: as an adverb before an adjective it softens degree ("relatively, quite" — 比较贵), but as a verb it means the literal action "to compare" (比较两者, "compare the two") — one word covering both a hedge and a concrete action.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 婚 relates to marriage, historically centered on the wife.
昏 (hūn) gives the sound — an exact match with 婚.
礻 (spirit, altar) — 礼 relates to ceremony and rites performed before the spirits.
乚 reflects the character's phonetic root, though its exact link to the modern reading lǐ is unclear today.

example.hanzi: 他们的婚礼办得很热闹。
example.pinyin: Tāmen de hūnlǐ bàn de hěn rènao.
example.english: Their wedding was lively and lots of fun.
example.fact: 礼 (ceremony, rite, courtesy) is one of Chinese's most productive roots for social-occasion vocabulary — it also builds 礼物 ("gift"), 礼貌 ("manners"), and 葬礼 ("funeral"), each pairing 礼 with the specific occasion it governs.

example.hanzi: 我弟弟比我小三岁。
example.pinyin: Wǒ dìdi bǐ wǒ xiǎo sān suì.
example.english: My younger brother is three years younger than me.
example.fact: Chinese kinship terms are strictly age- and gender-marked with no single word for "brother" the way English has one: 哥哥 (older brother), 弟弟 (younger brother), 姐姐 (older sister), and 妹妹 (younger sister, also in this batch) are four separate, non-interchangeable words.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — 组 originally meant 'to weave, arrange,' extended to 'group, to organize.'
且 (qiě) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zǔ.
纟 (thread) — 织 relates directly to weaving thread into fabric
只 (zhī) gives the sound — 织 is also pronounced zhī, an exact match

example.hanzi: 这个组织帮助了很多穷人。
example.pinyin: Zhège zǔzhī bāngzhùle hěn duō qióngrén.
example.english: This organization has helped many poor people.
example.fact: 组织 spans three distinct domains without changing form: a social "organization" (这个组织), the verb "to organize" (组织活动, "organize an event"), and in biology, "tissue" (肌肉组织, "muscle tissue") — one word doing the conceptual work of three unrelated English terms.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 想 relates to thinking, missing someone, or wanting something in one's heart.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — 想 is pronounced xiǎng, matching aside from tone.
心 (heart/mind) — 想 relates to thinking, missing someone, or wanting something in one's heart.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — 想 is pronounced xiǎng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 让我想想。
example.pinyin: Ràng wǒ xiǎngxiang.
example.english: Let me think about it.
example.fact: Like many one-syllable action verbs, 想 can reduplicate to soften a suggestion or request, making it feel lighter or more tentative — 想想 and its fuller variant 想一想 (with 一 inserted in the middle) are used interchangeably to mean "have a little think about it."

components.note: 冂 (a simplified eye shape in 见's modern form) — emphasizes the act of seeing.
儿 (a person) — a person with an emphasized eye above gives 见 its meaning 'to see.'
面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'

example.hanzi: 我们明天见面吧。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen míngtiān jiànmiàn ba.
example.english: Let's meet up tomorrow.
example.fact: 见面 is a verb-object compound (见 "see" + 面 "face") that's already grammatically complete on its own — it can't take a second object the way English "meet" can ("meet him"), so Chinese has to route the other person through 跟 or 和 instead: 跟他见面, never 见面他.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.
巾 (cloth) — 常 originally referred to a long skirt or banner made of cloth, later coming to mean something 'usual' or 'ordinary.'
尚 (shàng) gives a hint of the sound — 常 is pronounced cháng, a connection that has drifted over time.

example.hanzi: 她经常一个人去图书馆。
example.pinyin: Tā jīngcháng yí gè rén qù túshūguǎn.
example.english: She often goes to the library by herself.
example.fact: 经常 leans toward describing a regular, established habit ("on a regular basis"), while its near-synonym 常常 feels a touch more conversational and can describe a repeated pattern without implying it's routine — a nuance that surfaces mostly in formal writing, which prefers 经常.

components.note: 土 (earth) — relates to 城's meaning 'city, wall,' since city walls were built of earth.
成 (chéng) gives the sound — 城 is also pronounced chéng, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 上海是中国最大的城市之一。
example.pinyin: Shànghǎi shì Zhōngguó zuì dà de chéngshì zhī yī.
example.english: Shanghai is one of China's biggest cities.
example.fact: In ancient China a settlement wasn't a full "city" without both halves of this word in place: 城 named the defensive wall enclosing it, and 市 named the marketplace inside — 城市 fuses "the walled place" and "the market" into the modern general word for "city."

meanings: variant of 老闆|老板[lao3 ban3]

components.note: 耂 (a person bent with age, with long hair) — depicts an elderly figure.
匕 (here representing a cane or walking stick) — combined with the bent figure above, 老 pictures an old person leaning on a cane.
木 (wood) — boards and planks like 板 are traditionally made of wood.
反 (fǎn) gives a rhyme close to bǎn, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 我得问问老板才能请假。
example.pinyin: Wǒ děi wènwen lǎobǎn cái néng qǐngjià.
example.english: I have to ask my boss before I can take time off.
example.fact: 老 in 老板 isn't marking age at all — it's a common familiarizing prefix Chinese attaches to words for social roles and relations (老师 "teacher", 老婆 "wife", also in this batch) to make them feel warmer or more established, regardless of how old the person actually is.

components.note: 亻 (person) plus 乍 (suddenly/for the first time) — together suggesting a person making or doing something for the first time.

example.hanzi: 两家公司决定合作开发新产品。
example.pinyin: Liǎng jiā gōngsī juédìng hézuò kāifā xīn chǎnpǐn.
example.english: The two companies decided to collaborate on developing a new product.
example.fact: 合作's second character 作 ("to do, to make") is easy to confuse with the near-homophone 做, which covers most everyday "do/make" situations (做饭, "cook") — 作 survives mainly in set compounds and more literary or abstract verbs like 合作, 创作 ("to create"), and 工作 ("work"), rather than in casual daily speech.

components.note: Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 火车终于来到了车站。
example.pinyin: Huǒchē zhōngyú láidào le chēzhàn.
example.english: The train finally arrived at the station.
example.fact: 到 functions here as a resultative complement rather than an independent verb — attached after a motion verb it marks that the movement actually reached its destination, the same pattern seen in 回到 ("return to") and 走到 ("walk to"), where the first verb gives the manner and 到 nails down the result.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
人 (people) over 云 (clouds/say) — a picture of people gathering and speaking together, related to 会's meanings 'to meet' and 'to know how to.'
儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

example.hanzi: 你等一会儿,我马上就来。
example.pinyin: Nǐ děng yíhuìr, wǒ mǎshàng jiù lái.
example.english: Wait a moment, I'll be right there.
example.fact: 一会儿 doubles as a repeated pattern to describe alternating states: 一会儿哭,一会儿笑 ("crying one moment, laughing the next") uses two 一会儿's back to back to mean rapid, unstable switching — quite different from its plainer single use meaning just "a short while."

components.note: 羊 (sheep) — work involving livestock, done imperfectly
工 (work) — the labor itself, linked to the idea of falling short
The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
夕 (evening/night), doubled — two nights stacked together suggested the idea of accumulation, giving 多 its meaning of 'many, much.'

example.hanzi: 这两件衣服的价格差不多。
example.pinyin: Zhè liǎng jiàn yīfu de jiàgé chàbuduō.
example.english: These two pieces of clothing are about the same price.
example.fact: 差不多 is transparently built from its own literal meaning: 差 ("to differ, to fall short") + 不 ("not") + 多 ("much") spells out "not differing by much" — a rare case where a common idiom-feeling phrase is exactly as literal as it looks.

components.note: 耂 (a person bent with age, with long hair) — depicts an elderly figure.
匕 (here representing a cane or walking stick) — combined with the bent figure above, 老 pictures an old person leaning on a cane.
女 (woman) — 婆 names an older woman.
波 (bō) gives a sound close to pó, sharing the same rhyme.

example.hanzi: 我老婆做的菜特别好吃。
example.pinyin: Wǒ lǎopo zuò de cài tèbié hǎochī.
example.english: My wife's cooking is especially delicious.
example.fact: 老婆 is warm, colloquial, and mainly spoken — the neutral, written-register word for "wife" is 妻子. Like 老板 elsewhere in this batch, its 老 prefix signals familiarity rather than age, attached to 婆, a root that on its own can simply mean "old woman."

components.note: A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'
心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.

example.hanzi: 这家购物中心非常大。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gòuwù zhōngxīn fēicháng dà.
example.english: This shopping center is huge.
example.fact: 中心 layers a spatial "center" (中, the middle of a space) over a metaphorical one (心, literally "heart", the seat of core importance) — the same two-layer logic English uses when it calls something both the "center" of a city and the "heart" of a city.

components.note: 丁 (a stylized handle/hook shape in the ancient form) — part of the character's original picture, now mostly opaque in the modern form
口 (kǒu, mouth) gives a sound related to 可's pronunciation kě, and may connect to 可's sense of approval spoken aloud
忄 (heart) — 怕 relates to a feeling of fear in one's heart
白 (bái) gives a loose sound connection to 怕's reading pà

example.hanzi: 昨晚的暴风雨真可怕。
example.pinyin: Zuówǎn de bàofēngyǔ zhēn kěpà.
example.english: Last night's storm was really terrifying.
example.fact: 可 plus a verb is one of Mandarin's most productive adjective-building patterns: 可怕 ("fear-able" → "scary"), 可爱 ("love-able" → "cute"), and 可怜 (elsewhere in this batch, "pity-able" → "pitiful") all turn a verb into "worthy of [that reaction]" by simply prefixing 可.

components.note: 日 (sun) — combined with 月 (moon), 明 shows the light of both sun and moon, giving the meaning 'bright' or 'clear.'
月 (moon) — together with 日 (sun), the two brightest things in the sky represent brightness and clarity.
日 (sun) — 显 relates to something bright and clearly visible in the light
业 (yè) gives a loose sound connection to 显's reading xiǎn

example.hanzi: 他今天明显不高兴。
example.pinyin: Tā jīntiān míngxiǎn bù gāoxìng.
example.english: He's clearly not happy today.
example.fact: 明显 can modify an entire following clause as a sentence-level adverb, roughly like English "clearly" or "obviously" at the front of a sentence, rather than only describing a single noun — a flexible role many two-character adjectives pick up once they stand directly before a verb.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 研's meaning 'to grind, study closely' relates to grinding a stone to refine or research something.
开 (kāi) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from yán.
穴 (cave/hole) — 究's meaning 'to explore deeply, investigate' has been linked to exploring a cave.
九 (jiǔ) gives a sound hint — 究 is pronounced jiū, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 他在大学研究中国历史。
example.pinyin: Tā zài dàxué yánjiū Zhōngguó lìshǐ.
example.english: He researches Chinese history at university.
example.fact: 研究 lends its first character to 研究生 ("graduate student"), which literally reads as "research student" — a transparent coinage that maps the Chinese term for advanced academic study directly onto the activity itself, unlike the more opaque English "graduate."

meanings: (usu. followed by 到[dao4]) to be aware of

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.
讠 (speech) — relates to 识's meaning 'to know, recognize,' knowledge conveyed through words.
只 (zhǐ) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from shí.

example.hanzi: 他没有意识到自己犯了错误。
example.pinyin: Tā méiyǒu yìshí dào zìjǐ fànle cuòwù.
example.english: He didn't realize he had made a mistake.
example.fact: 意识 usually needs the complement 到 attached after it to mean "to become aware of / realize" (意识到) — used bare, without 到, 意识 functions instead as a plain noun meaning "consciousness," as in 失去意识 ("to lose consciousness").

components.note: 阝 (a mound, a place) — 附 relates to being near or attached to a place.
付 (fù) gives the sound — an exact match with 附.
辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 近's meaning 'near, close,' a short distance to walk.
斤 (jīn) gives a sound hint — 近 is pronounced jìn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 我家附近有一家超市。
example.pinyin: Wǒ jiā fùjìn yǒu yì jiā chāoshì.
example.english: There's a supermarket near my home.
example.fact: 附近 behaves grammatically like a place noun rather than a preposition — it follows 在 and a location the same way 里面 ("inside") or 上面 ("on top") do, so "near my house" is 我家附近 or 在我家附近, never a bare preposition directly modifying "house" the way English "near" would.

components.note: 凡 (common/ordinary) — suggests something shared or held in common.
口 (mouth) — sharing a common mouth/voice with others gave 同 its meaning of 'same, together.'
忄 (heart/mind) — 性 relates to inner nature or character.
生 (shēng) gives a hint of the sound — 性 is pronounced xìng, a related sound though the initial has shifted.
心 (heart) — 恋 describes a heart drawn to and longing for someone or something.
亦 (yì) is only distantly related in sound to liàn — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.hanzi: 越来越多的国家承认同性恋婚姻合法。
example.pinyin: Yuèláiyuè duō de guójiā chéngrèn tóngxìngliàn hūnyīn héfǎ.
example.english: More and more countries recognize same-sex marriage as legal.
example.fact: 同性恋 is the standard clinical-sounding term found in dictionaries and law; contemporary LGBTQ+ community usage in Chinese more often reaches for 同志 ("comrade"), a Communist-era term that was reclaimed as an in-group, affectionate label starting in Hong Kong in the late 1980s.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 打 relates to hitting or performing an action with the hand.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — 打 is pronounced dǎ, a connection that has shifted in tone.
扌 (hand) — 扰 describes stirring something up by hand, 'to disturb.'
尤 (yóu) is only distantly related in sound to rǎo — the connection has drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 打扰一下,请问洗手间在哪儿?
example.pinyin: Dǎrǎo yíxià, qǐngwèn xǐshǒujiān zài nǎr?
example.english: Excuse me, where is the restroom?
example.fact: 打扰一下 ("sorry to bother you for a second") functions as a fixed politeness formula for interrupting a stranger, playing a role very close to English "excuse me" — swapping in 打扰您 instead of 你 raises the same phrase to a more respectful register.

components.note: 女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 运's meaning 'to move, transport,' and by extension 'fortune,' the movement of one's life.
云 (yún) gives a sound hint — 运 is pronounced yùn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 祝你好运!
example.pinyin: Zhù nǐ hǎoyùn!
example.english: Wish you good luck!
example.fact: 好运 is a shortened, punchier form of the fuller noun phrase 好运气 ("good luck/fortune") — dropping 气 lets it work as a snappy, stand-alone exclamation, the way English clips "good fortune" down to just "luck" in casual speech.

components.note: 纟 (thread) — relates directly to 线's meaning 'line, thread, wire.'
戋 (jiān) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from xiàn.
糸 (thread) — thick strands twisted into a rope
冖 (a covering) — the ceiling or beam the rope hangs from

example.hanzi: 警察还没找到任何线索。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá hái méi zhǎodào rènhé xiànsuǒ.
example.english: The police haven't found any clues yet.
example.fact: Both halves of 线索 independently mean a strand of some kind — 线 ("thread, line") and 索 (literally a twisted cord, per its own 糸 "thread" and 冖 "covering" components) — so 线索 builds "clue" the same way English metaphorically "follows a thread" of an investigation.

components.note: 面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'

example.hanzi: 他在老师面前不敢说谎。
example.pinyin: Tā zài lǎoshī miànqián bù gǎn shuōhuǎng.
example.english: He doesn't dare lie in front of his teacher.
example.fact: 面前 specifically frames being in a person's direct presence or view (老师面前, "in the teacher's presence") — for plain physical, spatial "in front of" with no implication of anyone watching, Chinese instead reaches for the more general 前面 (前面有一家商店, "there's a shop up ahead").

components.note: 氵 (water) — relates to 消's meaning 'to disappear, dissolve,' like something dissolving in water.
肖 (xiào) gives a sound hint — 消 is pronounced xiāo, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
丿 (something falling) — an object slipping away.
夫 (a hand/person) — the object slipping out of a hand, giving 失 its meaning 'to lose.'

example.hanzi: 那只猫突然消失了。
example.pinyin: Nà zhī māo tūrán xiāoshī le.
example.english: That cat suddenly disappeared.
example.fact: 消失 layers two images of loss: 消 (built on the water radical 氵, "to dissolve, melt away") plus 失 ("to lose, to slip from one's grasp") — together painting "vanish" as something dissolving right out of your hands.

components.note: 女 (woman) — 妹 names a female relative, a younger sister.
未 (wèi) gives a rhyme close to mèi, with a different initial.
女 (woman) — 妹 names a female relative, a younger sister.
未 (wèi) gives a rhyme close to mèi, with a different initial.

example.hanzi: 我妹妹在读高中。
example.pinyin: Wǒ mèimei zài dú gāozhōng.
example.english: My younger sister is in high school.
example.fact: Beyond its literal family sense, 妹 by itself has become a casual, often internet-influenced way to refer to a young woman or girl in general (小妹, 萌妹) — much like English "sis" can address a young woman with no real sibling relationship implied.

components.note: 一 (a line, representing a target or standard) — 正 shows a foot arriving exactly at the right mark.
止 (foot, to stop) — arriving and stopping precisely at the target gives 正 its meaning of 'correct' or 'straight.'
石 (stone) — 确 originally meant firm and solid like stone, extending to 'true, accurate, indeed.'
角 (jiǎo) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from què.

example.hanzi: 你的答案是正确的。
example.pinyin: Nǐ de dá'àn shì zhèngquè de.
example.english: Your answer is correct.
example.fact: 正确 is the formal, written-register word for "correct"; in casual speech, Chinese usually reaches for the shorter 对 instead ("对, 你说得对", "right, you're right") — 正确 shows up far more often on tests, in official statements, and in writing than in relaxed conversation.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 位 relates to a person's location.
立 (to stand) — the spot where a person stands gave 位 its meaning 'position' or 'place,' and later, a polite measure word for people.
罒 (a net) — 置 originally meant to set a net in place
直 (zhí) gives a sound close to 置's reading zhì, sharing a similar historical pronunciation

example.hanzi: 请把箱子放在原来的位置。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ xiāngzi fàng zài yuánlái de wèizhi.
example.english: Please put the box back in its original place.
example.fact: 位置 covers both a literal spot (座位的位置, "the seat's location") and an abstract one — a person's standing or rank in a hierarchy — mirroring the same literal-to-figurative jump English makes with the word "position."

example.hanzi: 妈妈答应带我去公园。
example.pinyin: Māma dāying dài wǒ qù gōngyuán.
example.english: Mom promised to take me to the park.
example.fact: 答 is usually read dá (回答 "to answer", 答案 "answer") but switches to the lighter-sounding dā specifically in 答应 — one of a handful of characters that quietly change reading depending on which word they're locked into, a trap worth memorizing case by case rather than assuming one fixed pronunciation.

components.note: 电 (simplified from 電) depicts a bolt of lightning — since lightning is a natural form of electricity, the character came to mean 'electricity.'
⺼ (flesh/body) — 脑 refers to the brain, a part of the body

example.hanzi: 我的电脑坏了,需要修。
example.pinyin: Wǒ de diànnǎo huài le, xūyào xiū.
example.english: My computer is broken and needs to be fixed.
example.fact: 电脑, literally "electric brain" (电 "electricity" + 脑 "brain"), is Mainland China and Taiwan's everyday word for "computer" — more technical and academic writing also uses the more literal 计算机 ("calculating machine"), roughly the difference in English between casual "computer" and formal "computing machine."

components.note: 亻 (a person), shown twice — one person next to another, similar in shape, the source of 似's meaning 'to resemble, similar, like.'

example.hanzi: 他似乎不太满意这个结果。
example.pinyin: Tā sìhū bú tài mǎnyì zhège jiéguǒ.
example.english: He doesn't seem too satisfied with this result.
example.fact: 似乎 is a bookish, written-register hedge word; in everyday spoken Chinese, 好像 ("seems like") fills almost the same role but sounds noticeably more casual — the kind of pair where reaching for the wrong one flags a text as either overly stiff or too informal.

components.note: 攵 (a hand with an implement, action) — relates to 放's meaning 'to let go, release, put.'
方 (fāng) gives the sound — 放 is pronounced fàng, a close match sharing the same rhyme.
A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.hanzi: 他终于放下了心中的怨恨。
example.pinyin: Tā zhōngyú fàngxiàle xīnzhōng de yuànhèn.
example.english: He finally let go of the resentment in his heart.
example.fact: 放下 extends its literal meaning ("put down, lay down") into an emotional metaphor for letting go — 放下心 ("set one's mind at ease") and 放下过去 ("let go of the past") both use the same physical verb to describe releasing an emotional burden, much like English "put it down" or "let it go."

components.note: 力 depicts the blade of a plow — since plowing fields took great physical effort, the shape came to represent strength or power.
里 (a unit of distance, related to a village measure) — 量 relates to measuring quantity.
旦 (dàn) gives a hint of the sound — 量 is pronounced liàng, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 团结就是力量。
example.pinyin: Tuánjié jiùshì lìliang.
example.english: Unity is strength.
example.fact: 力量 usually names an abstract or collective force — physical, political, or emotional strength (精神力量, "spiritual strength") — while its near-synonym 力气 stays narrowly physical, the concrete muscle-power a single body has or lacks (没有力气, "to have no energy left").

components.note: 令 (an order, command) — 命 pictures issuing a command.
口 (mouth) — a command given aloud gave 命 its meaning 'order' or 'decree,' and by extension, 'fate' or 'life.'
人 (a person) — kneeling before a figure of authority, the image of receiving an order that gave 令 its meaning 'command, order; to cause.'

example.hanzi: 士兵必须服从命令。
example.pinyin: Shìbīng bìxū fúcóng mìnglìng.
example.english: Soldiers must obey orders.
example.fact: 命令 reinforces two near-synonymous halves into one word, much like 喜欢 and 应该 elsewhere in this deck: 命 alone already carries the sense of a decree spoken aloud (per its 口 "mouth" component), and 令 independently pictures a person kneeling to receive an order — together doubling down on the same core image.

components.note: 凡 (common/ordinary) — suggests something shared or held in common.
口 (mouth) — sharing a common mouth/voice with others gave 同 its meaning of 'same, together.'
日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form

example.hanzi: 两人同时到达了机场。
example.pinyin: Liǎng rén tóngshí dàodá le jīchǎng.
example.english: The two of them arrived at the airport at the same time.
example.fact: 同时 doubles as both a time adverb ("at the same time," 他们同时开始) and a sentence connector meaning roughly "moreover, besides" (同时,他也很努力, "moreover, he's also hardworking") — a shift from marking simultaneity to marking additional information.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 提 relates to lifting or carrying something by hand.
是 (shì) gives a hint of the sound — 提 is pronounced tí, a connection that has shifted over time.
亻 (person) — the one making an offering.
共 (together/both hands) — a person offering something with both hands gave 供 its meaning 'to supply, provide, offer.'

example.hanzi: 学校为学生提供免费午餐。
example.pinyin: Xuéxiào wèi xuésheng tígōng miǎnfèi wǔcān.
example.english: The school provides free lunch for students.
example.fact: 提供 typically marks the recipient with 为 or 给 rather than stacking two objects directly after the verb — 为学生提供午餐 or 提供午餐给学生, but not a bare double-object 提供学生午餐 — a pattern worth drilling since English "provide someone something" allows exactly the structure Chinese avoids here.

components.note: 戌 (a halberd/weapon) — represents armed force.
女 (woman) — force used to intimidate gave 威 its meaning 'power, might, awe-inspiring.'
办 (to manage, to handle) — 胁 describes exerting control over someone.
⺼ (flesh/body) — controlling 办 another's body ⺼ gave 胁 its meaning 'to threaten, to coerce.'

example.hanzi: 气候变化威胁着许多动物的生存。
example.pinyin: Qìhòu biànhuà wēixiézhe xǔduō dòngwù de shēngcún.
example.english: Climate change is threatening the survival of many animals.
example.fact: 威胁's two halves independently point toward force applied to a body: 威 combines a weapon 戌 with 女 to suggest armed intimidation, while 胁 (built on the flesh radical ⺼) evokes controlling someone physically, close to its literal meaning "ribs/flank" — together painting coercive threat as bodily domination.
